title: PHP Frameworks & APIs
intro: This term you move from plain PHP to Laravel, a real framework used by working developers. Step by step you will build an online shop with its own API and a safe Paystack test checkout.
termProject: ChopNow: an online store for a local Ilaro caterer (jollof, moi moi, small chops) in Laravel, with a menu API, naira-to-dollar prices and a Paystack TEST-mode checkout.

weeks.title: Laravel: your shop's front gate
weeks.goal: Set up a Laravel project and make three routes that answer different web addresses.
weeks.learn: A framework is a ready-made kitchen: the pots, gas and shelves are already there, so you just cook. Laravel is a PHP framework that gives you that kitchen for websites. A route is like the gate-man at an owambe: when a guest comes to a door like /menu, he decides who serves them. In Laravel, all your doors live in routes/web.php.

research.q: Ask a caterer or food seller: what are the first three things a new customer asks you?
research.tip: Write each question down; each one can become a page (a route) on your shop website.

research.tip: If prices change often, that is why we keep data in the controller, not typed into the page.

weeks.title: Talking to other computers: APIs
weeks.goal: Fetch live weather from a free public API with PHP and make a decision with it.
weeks.learn: An API is like a POS agent: you send a clear request, and you get a clear answer back. Many APIs answer in JSON, a neat list of names and values. PHP can call an API with file_get_contents and turn JSON into an array with json_decode. Open-Meteo is free and needs no key or personal data.

research.q: Ask a caterer or farmer: how does the weather change your work on an event day?
research.tip: Write one weather rule they use, like 'if it rains, we cover the canopy', and code it.

build.task: Get Ilaro's current temperature from Open-Meteo and print advice for an outdoor party.
steps: Copy the code into weather.php
Run: php weather.php in the terminal
Read the temperature it prints

build.code:
<?php
// weather.php  (Open-Meteo: free, no key needed)
$url = 'https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=6.89&longitude=3.01&current_weather=true';

$json = @file_get_contents($url);
if ($json === false) {
    exit("No network. Try again later.\n");
}

$data = json_decode($json, true);
$temp = $data['current_weather']['temperature'];

echo "Ilaro now: {$temp}°C\n";
if ($temp >= 32) {
    echo "Very hot! Keep the small chops in the shade.\n";
} elseif ($temp >= 25) {
    echo "Warm. Good day for an owambe.\n";
} else {
    echo "Cool weather. Bring out the pepper soup!\n";
}

weeks.title: Build your own API
weeks.goal: Create RESTful API routes in Laravel that return the menu as JSON.
weeks.learn: Last week we used someone's API; today we build our own. REST means using clear addresses for things, like /api/dishes for all dishes and /api/dishes/2 for one dish. Laravel turns PHP arrays into JSON with response()->json. A good API also says when something is missing with code 404, like a seller saying 'it has finished'.

research.q: Ask a caterer: if a phone app could ask your shop one question, what should it ask?
research.tip: Each answer is a possible API address, like /api/dishes or /api/today-special.

build.task: Make GET /api/dishes and GET /api/dishes/{id} that return JSON, with a 404 for unknown dishes.
steps: Laravel 11+: run php artisan install:api once
Paste the code into routes/api.php
Visit /api/dishes and /api/dishes/1
Try /api/dishes/9 and see the 404 message
build.code:
<?php
// routes/api.php
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

$dishes = [
    1 => ['name' => 'Jollof Rice', 'price' => 1500],
    2 => ['name' => 'Moi Moi', 'price' => 500],
    3 => ['name' => 'Small Chops', 'price' => 2000],
];

Route::get('/dishes', fn () => response()->json($dishes));

Route::get('/dishes/{id}', function ($id) use ($dishes) {
    if (!isset($dishes[$id])) {
        return response()->json(['error' => 'Dish not found'], 404);
    }
    return response()->json($dishes[$id]);
});

weeks.title: API that saves: create, update, delete
weeks.goal: Use a database model so the API can add, change and remove dishes.
weeks.learn: A full REST API has four main actions: GET to read, POST to add, PUT to change and DELETE to remove. To remember data, we use a database table and a Laravel model called Dish. It is like the caterer's notebook: new dishes are written in, prices are crossed out and changed. We test with a tool like Thunder Client or Postman.

research.q: Ask a trader: how often do you change prices, and who is allowed to change them?
research.tip: This tells us which API actions need protection, like only the owner can PUT a new price.

build.task: Make a Dish model and API routes to list, add, update and delete dishes.
steps: Run: php artisan make:model Dish -m
Add name and price columns in the migration, then php artisan migrate
Add $fillable to the model and paste the routes
Test POST, PUT and DELETE with Thunder Client
build.code:
<?php
// app/Models/Dish.php  ->  protected $fillable = ['name', 'price'];
// routes/api.php
use App\Models\Dish;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::get('/dishes', fn () => Dish::all());

Route::post('/dishes', function (Request $r) {
    $data = $r->validate(['name' => 'required', 'price' => 'required|integer|min:0']);
    return response()->json(Dish::create($data), 201);
});

Route::put('/dishes/{dish}', function (Request $r, Dish $dish) {
    $dish->update($r->validate(['price' => 'required|integer|min:0']));
    return $dish;
});

Route::delete('/dishes/{dish}', function (Dish $dish) {
    $dish->delete();
    return response()->noContent();
});

opts: To say which fields can be filled from a request

weeks.title: Tidy kitchen: services and config
weeks.goal: Move business logic into a service class and settings into config so the app can grow.
weeks.learn: A small buka can keep everything on one table, but a big catering company has a store, a kitchen and a cashier. Scalable code is organised the same way. A service class does one job, like working out the order total. Settings like the delivery fee go in config and .env, so you change them in one place without touching code.

research.q: Ask a caterer: what costs change between jobs, like delivery, gas or extra staff?
research.tip: Each changing cost should be a setting in config, not a number buried in your code.

build.task: Create an OrderService that totals a cart and adds a delivery fee from config.

build.code:
<?php
// app/Services/OrderService.php
namespace App\Services;

class OrderService
{
    public function total(array $items): int
    {
        $sum = 0;
        foreach ($items as $item) {
            $sum += $item['price'] * $item['qty'];
        }
        return $sum + config('shop.delivery_fee');
    }
}

weeks.title: Borrowing other services: exchange rates
weeks.goal: Use Laravel's HTTP client and cache to show naira prices in US dollars from a free service.
weeks.learn: Big apps don't build everything; they borrow from other services, like a caterer hiring chairs instead of buying them. Laravel's Http::get calls another service easily. Rates don't change every second, so Cache::remember keeps the answer for an hour, saving data and time. Always plan for when the service is down.

research.q: Ask a family member or neighbour: which outside services does your business use, like POS, delivery riders or chair rental?
research.tip: This shows why apps also use outside services, and what happens when one fails.

build.task: Add a page that converts a naira price to US dollars using open.er-api.com.
steps: Paste the route into routes/web.php
Visit /price-in-dollars/5000
Visit again and notice it is faster (cached)
Turn off Wi-Fi, clear cache, and see the friendly error
build.code:
<?php
// routes/web.php
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Cache;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Http;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::get('/price-in-dollars/{naira}', function (int $naira) {
    try {
        $rates = Cache::remember('ngn_rates', 3600, function () {
            return Http::timeout(5)->get('https://open.er-api.com/v6/latest/NGN')->json();
        });
    } catch (\Exception $e) {
        return 'Rate service is not reachable. Try again later.';
    }

    if (($rates['result'] ?? '') !== 'success') {
        Cache::forget('ngn_rates');
        return 'Rate service is down. Try again later.';
    }

    $usd = round($naira * $rates['rates']['USD'], 2);
    return "₦{$naira} is about \${$usd}";
});

check.q: Why do we cache the rates?
What should your app do if the service is down?

weeks.title: Paystack test checkout (no real money!)
weeks.goal: Connect a Paystack TEST checkout to the shop and confirm the payment on return.
weeks.learn: A payment gateway like Paystack is a trusted cashier between the buyer and the shop. Paystack gives two kinds of keys: test keys (sk_test_...) for practice, where no real money moves, and live keys for real business. In class we use ONLY test keys, and we never put any key in our code or on GitHub: it stays in .env. Paystack counts money in kobo, so ₦3,500 is 350000.

research.q: Ask a shop owner who uses POS or transfers: how do you confirm a customer has really paid?
research.tip: Their answer explains why our app must verify every payment with Paystack, not just trust the customer.

build.task: Send a test order to Paystack's test checkout, then verify it when the customer returns.
steps: Create a free Paystack account and copy ONLY the test secret key
Put it in .env and add it to config/services.php
Paste the routes and make a form that POSTs to /pay with @csrf
Pay with a test card from Paystack's docs and check /paid
build.code:
<?php
// .env -> PAYSTACK_SECRET=sk_test_...   (TEST key only. Never a live key. Never commit .env)
// config/services.php -> 'paystack' => ['secret' => env('PAYSTACK_SECRET')],
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Http;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::post('/pay', function () {
    $res = Http::withToken(config('services.paystack.secret'))
        ->post('https://api.paystack.co/transaction/initialize', [
            'email'        => 'test-buyer@example.com', // dummy email, never a real child's email
            'amount'       => 3500 * 100,               // kobo: ₦3,500
            'callback_url' => url('/paid'),
        ]);
    return redirect($res->json('data.authorization_url'));
});

Route::get('/paid', function () {
    $ref = urlencode(request('reference', ''));
    $check = Http::withToken(config('services.paystack.secret'))
        ->get("https://api.paystack.co/transaction/verify/{$ref}");
    return $check->json('data.status') === 'success'
        ? 'Test payment confirmed! (No real money moved.)'
        : 'Payment not confirmed.';
});
